title: CBA mortgage arrears rise to 14-year high
full_text:
The Commonwealth Bank has increased its provisions for bad debts, and mortgage arrears rose to their highest level since 2012, as falling house prices and a weakening economy failed to offset stronger business lending.
Australia's largest lender reported a first-quarter cash profit of $2.8 billion, an 8 per cent increase on the same quarter last year, as it continued to win share of business loans.
But the quarterly update pointed to slowing growth momentum, as profit was flat when measured against the bank's performance earlier this year.
"Higher inflation and interest rates continue to place uneven pressure on household incomes and business activity," said chief executive Matt Comyn in a statement to the ASX.
Home loan arrears rose by 7 basis points during the quarter, an increase attributed to rising cost of living pressures, bringing the rate of customers more than 90 days late on their mortgage to 0.80 per cent.
A chart released on Tuesday showed this at a six-year-high - but the last time this metric was above 0.8 per cent was in 2012, 14 years ago, according to previous CBA market updates. The bank said it had been slower to resolve delinquencies, allowing for longer paused collection against borrowers.
The loan loss rate of 11 basis points was up 3 basis points over the quarter - but well below the average level for the decade before COVID-19.
CBA home loan applications were down 16 per cent quarter on quarter after tax concession changes in the federal budget and consecutive interest rate rises. Still, CBA home lending grew 6.6 per cent year on year, broadly in line with system growth, while deposits were up 7.7 per cent.
The bank recorded a loan impairment expense of $300 million, broadly in line with the May quarter. It increased its collective provisions - money set aside to cover potential losses if borrowers are unable to pay - by $105 million in the quarter, which it said was because of house price falls.
The bank's economists do not expect house prices to bottom until late next year, at which time they estimate the average value of a home will have fallen 15 per cent across the capital cities. CBA shares traded 0.8 per cent up at the open to hover at about $170.30 a share before giving back its gains at about 11am.
JPMorgan analyst Andrew Triggs expected the softer spots in the update lead to slight downgrades in 2027 financial year cash profit forecasts for CBA as impairments rose, and the swaps that have protected the bank's tier-one capital ratio began to unwind.
VanEck senior portfolio manager Cameron McCormack said CBA shares were highly priced and investors were expecting the business to deliver superior results, "which we haven't seen in this update".
"Softer forward guidance and slowing mortgage demand could see CBA underperform the broader market over the coming months," McCormack said.
Comyn said that despite economic growth slowing, the Australian economy remained resilient, supported by low unemployment, and a strong public infrastructure and private investment pipeline.
The bank increased business lending by 13.6 per cent year on year, as it continued to take market share in that sector from rivals: Westpac grew business lending at 12 per cent, while NAB grew 9.8 per cent, as lenders compensated for a softer mortgage market.
"Business lending growth was well diversified across a range of sectors, supported by the strength of our proprietary customer relationships and continued business investment demand," said Comyn.
He said the bank maintained a strong balance sheet to "navigate a range of economic conditions".
CBA's quarterly update rounds out a fortnight of big bank reporting that has turned a spotlight on the weaker economic outlook and the banks' responses to it, including higher provision levels. All the major banks lifted impairment charges last financial year, according to KPMG's analysis of the banks' accounts.
CBA's total provisions for its first quarter were flat at $6.5 billion, as higher collective provisions were offset by lower individual provisions for corporate exposures.
